extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for forming and evaluating inductive inferences, probability assessments, classifications (kinds), and generalizations in scientific and philosophical argument. Emphasizes the role of causes, limits of frequency-only reasoning, and proper conceptual framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer probabilities via causes, not solely from raw frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not ... conclude directly from the happening of an event to the probability of its happening again; but that we refer to the cause, regarding the past cases as an index to the cause, and the cause as our guide to the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past frequencies serve as an index to the underlying cause(s); probability for future occurrence should be based on knowledge of the cause(s) and whether those causes will persist. Example: insurance and business of life rely on frequency because they index stable causes; if causes change (a change in the 'collocation of causes'), inference from past frequency fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of frequency-only valuation of chances
rubrics_metrics.description: The valuation of chances by comparing the number of cases in which the event occurs with the number in which it does not occur 'would generally be wholly erroneous' if taken without regard to causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequency counts can mislead when they ignore differing causal contexts or changing conditions. The author defends frequency-based methods (e.g., insurance) only where they reflect stable causal arrangements; one must check for intervening changes that would invalidate extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict generalizations to the uniformity actually observed
rubrics_metrics.description: Early generalizations did not presuppose causation but uniformity in physical facts limited to observation; they assumed only as much uniformity beyond observation as corresponded to what had been proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not tacitly assume universal uniformity of nature. An induction like 'fire burns' requires uniformity only within that class of phenomena, not across all nature. The strength of a generalization should match the scope of observed uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define impossibility relative to complete induction
rubrics_metrics.description: An impossibility is that, the truth of which would conflict with a complete induction, that is, with the most conclusive evidence which we possess of universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition subsumes both logical impossibilities (2+2=5) and cases where no known cause can produce the effect; it warns against treating current ignorance as permanent impossibility by giving examples of formerly 'impossible' feats now achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify natural kinds by conjunctions of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: In some cases a Kind is sufficiently identified by some one remarkable property: but most commonly several are required; each property considered singly, being a joint property of that and of other Kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple independent properties together to mark a Kind (e.g., color, brightness, and form together identify a diamond). Single properties are often shared with other Kinds and insufficient for reliable classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply general canons of induction to causal and compositional claims
rubrics_metrics.description: All cases of chemical composition are cases of causation; the Canons of Induction, therefore, as laid down in this treatise, are applicable to the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat composition or chemical laws as outside causal inductive methods; special methodological adaptations belong to the logic of the special sciences, but general inductive principles still govern discovery and proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit conclusions drawn from approximate generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: From two such premises as 'Most A are B' and 'Most A are C' we may infer with certainty that some B are C; this is the utmost limit when the degrees of approximation to universality are unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about combining approximate generalizations: they do not justify strong joint inferences unless the degree of approximation is known. De Morgan's remark illustrates the maximal safe inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate chances by analyzing underlying causes' frequency and efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of frequency of a coincidence depends on, and is a measure of, the frequency, combined with the efficacy, of the causes in operation that are favorable to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing combined probabilities (e.g., items that are both A and C being B), analyze how each relevant set of causes operates separately and jointly. The text supplies a concrete numerical example (resulting in 11/12) showing how combined causal operations determine the overall chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish psychological presumption from logical proof in induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The resemblance of what we have not experienced to what we have is, by a law of our nature, presumed through the mere energy of the idea (psychological truth), but the logical truth that experience does prove it comes after, by invariable verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that humans hold a natural presumption of uniformity (psychology) which facilitates reasoning, but the epistemic warrant for generalizations is provided by repeated verification (logic/experience). Don't conflate the two when judging validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat alleged miracles as invoking new antecedent causes rather than exceptions to causation
rubrics_metrics.description: In every case of alleged miracle, a new antecedent is affirmed to exist; a counteracting cause, namely, the volition of a supernatural being. To those who accept such beings as vera causa, a miracle is a case of the Law of Universal Causation, not a deviation from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing reports of apparent law-violations, consider whether the report posits a new antecedent cause (thus preserving causation) instead of taking it as empirical counter-evidence to universal causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inappropriate or false conceptions when forming generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Inappropriate conceptions (using the wrong generalizing principle) and false conceptions (those with no prototype in nature) lead to failed explanations; examples include applying geometrical notions of the circle inappropriately to mechanics or optics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select principles of generalization that correspond to empirical prototypes and causal mechanisms; beware of metaphors or imported concepts that have no factual basis and will produce spurious inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concepts/names as practical tools for class-level induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The name of a class calls up some idea, through which we can, to all intents and purposes, think of the class as such, and not solely of an individual member of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceptual images of exemplar individuals can legitimately function as proxies to reason about classes; ensure the exemplar idea captures the relevant class features for the intended inductive inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute testimonial credibility by analyzing error rates and base-rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Credibility of an announcement should be evaluated by a full analysis of error rates and frequencies (example: mistaken announcements of a particular numbered draw vs the announcement 'white'); naive ratio estimates can be misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work through the combinatorics of truthful vs erroneous announcements rather than relying on superficial ratios. The text gives a detailed calculation showing how base-rate and error interact to change comparative credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer definitions that capture the essential attribute of a concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometers have usually preferred to define parallel lines by 'being in the same plane and never meeting', but equidistance is a fitter property to characterize parallels because it captures the attribute really involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose definitions that express the core essence (e.g., equidistance for parallels) rather than peripheral or derivative properties; this reduces the need for ad hoc axioms and yields clearer reasoning.
